title: Headache, Vomiting, and a Rock-Hard Eye

patient.name: Mdm Tan Geok Hwa
patient.presenting_complaint: Sudden severe left-sided headache with eye pain, blurred vision, nausea and vomiting that started about 3 hours ago while watching a movie in a dark cinema

history.hpc: Mdm Tan was watching a movie in a dark cinema about 3 hours ago when she developed a sudden severe headache on the left side, centred around and behind her left eye. The pain is severe (8/10) and she describes seeing 'rainbow halos' around the cinema lights before the pain started. She has vomited twice since. Her left eye vision is now very blurry — she describes it as 'looking through a steamed-up mirror'. She has never experienced this before. She is hyperopic (long-sighted) and has never had an eye examination for glaucoma.
history.pmhx: Hyperopia (long-sightedness), uncorrected. No known glaucoma history. Hypertension, well-controlled. No previous eye surgery.
history.family_hx: Mother had 'eye pressure problems' in old age, details unclear
history.social_hx: Works as a tailor — fine near work. Came in with her husband, who is very worried.

examination_findings.anterior_segment: Left eye: conjunctival hyperaemia (red eye), hazy/oedematous cornea, mid-dilated and fixed oval pupil unresponsive to light, anterior chamber appears shallow. Right eye: also appears to have a shallow anterior chamber on gross inspection, but quiet and comfortable.
examination_findings.fundus: Unable to assess left fundus due to corneal oedema. Right fundus not yet assessed.

investigations.iop_nct: RE: 19 mmHg. LE: 56 mmHg — markedly elevated, multiple readings consistent.
investigations.va_distance: RE: LogMAR 0.2 (6/9). LE: CF at 0.5m — unable to read LogMAR chart.
investigations.pain_assessment: 8/10 left peri-orbital and headache pain, associated with nausea and two episodes of vomiting — classic triad for acute angle closure glaucoma

diagnosis: Acute Angle-Closure Glaucoma (AACG), left eye, precipitated by pupil dilation in a dark environment (cinema) in a hyperopic patient with anatomically narrow angles. Triage Category 1 — must be seen by doctor within 10 minutes.

immediate: Recognise the classic triad of severe unilateral eye pain/headache + nausea/vomiting + sudden blurred vision as AACG until proven otherwise
Triage as Category 1 — alert the doctor immediately, patient must be seen within 10 minutes
Do NOT leave the patient unattended; keep her seated comfortably and calm
Measure VA and IOP in both eyes promptly — note the markedly elevated left IOP (56 mmHg) and very low VA
Document the precipitating factor (dark cinema environment) — relevant clinical clue for AACG
Do NOT instil any drops, including dilating drops, without the doctor's explicit order
Note the right eye's shallow anterior chamber on gross inspection and flag this — the right eye is also at risk and may need prophylactic treatment later
Document triage time, pain score, vomiting episodes, and all findings on the SNEC Triage Form
follow_up: Doctor will initiate emergency IOP-lowering treatment (e.g. IV acetazolamide, topical agents) for the left eye
Likely arrangement for laser peripheral iridotomy (LPI) once the acute attack is controlled
Right eye (also narrow angle) will likely need prophylactic LPI as well, to be discussed by doctor
Monitor patient closely, including repeat IOP checks as directed
patient_education: Reassure Mdm Tan and her husband that this is a recognised emergency and the team is acting quickly
Explain simply that the pressure inside her left eye has risen suddenly because the drainage angle has become blocked, often triggered by being in the dark
Advise her not to rub her eye and to remain seated calmly while waiting for the doctor
Explain that her right eye may need a preventive laser treatment later, since it has a similar anatomy

key_points: Identifies the classic AACG triad: severe pain/headache, nausea/vomiting, sudden blurred vision
Identifies the precipitating factor (dark cinema environment) as a relevant clue
Asks about hyperopia/refractive history (hyperopes have shallower anterior chambers, higher AACG risk)
Asks about prior similar episodes and family history of 'eye pressure problems'
Uses pain scale to document severity (8/10)
Measures VA in both eyes promptly (right normal, left severely reduced to CF)
Performs NCT and identifies markedly elevated left IOP (56 mmHg) consistent with AACG
Observes and documents the mid-dilated fixed pupil, corneal oedema, and shallow anterior chamber
Notes the right eye's anatomy (shallow anterior chamber) as relevant for future risk
Correctly identifies this as Acute Angle-Closure Glaucoma, left eye
Correctly assigns SNEC Triage Category 1 (within 10 minutes)
Recognises the precipitating role of pupil dilation in low light in a predisposed (hyperopic, narrow angle) patient
Recognises the fellow eye is also at risk and flags this appropriately
Alerts doctor immediately and does not delay for full documentation first
Does not instil any drops without doctor's order
Stays with the patient and keeps her calm and comfortable
Documents triage time and all findings completely on the SNEC Triage Form
Communicates the fellow-eye risk for follow-up planning
